# Background: cohesion and behavior in school classrooms

Van den Bos, Crone, Meuwese, and Güroğlu (2018) asked how adolescents' network
positions and classroom cohesion relate to peer-reported social behavior and
generalized trust. They recruited 611 students from 22 classes in one Dutch
secondary school, with a mean age of 14.8 years. They report excluding two
mixed classes whose membership changed over time, leaving 496 participants
(article, pp. 3 and 10).

Students nominated classmates they liked most, without a fixed nomination limit
and without self-nominations. Other questions measured helping, cooperation,
aggression, victimization, and perceived popularity. An economic game measured
trust in unfamiliar others. The authors used **mutual liking**: an undirected
edge existed only when both students nominated one another (pp. 3 and 10–11;
S2 Text, item 1).

The authors measured cohesion with mutual-network density, diameter, and
clusters. Denser mutual networks were associated with less antisocial behavior;
larger classes with more antisocial behavior. Fewer clusters and shorter
diameter were associated with greater generalized trust (pp. 5–6). At the
individual level, eigenvector centrality was associated with more prosocial
behavior and relational aggression and less victimization; no individual
centrality measure was associated with trust (pp. 7–8; Table 3 and S4).
The cross-sectional design does not identify causation (p. 9).

[Despite the title's wording, the authors describe the direct classroom-cohesion
association with prosocial behavior as a trend in the discussion (p. 9). I do
not present that as an established causal effect.]

**My application keeps the directions.** I use all sixteen released students in
archive group 36 to distinguish sending nominations, receiving nominations,
and residual reciprocity. I model neither helping nor trust, and I am not
replicating the paper's cross-classroom behavioral regressions.

[**Question:** How are liking nominations associated with matching recorded sex
and age differences, and what changes when I add multiplicative structure beyond
actor tendencies and residual reciprocity? By the end, I want to be able to
construct aligned network inputs, explain the two model calls, and interpret
results together with their diagnostics.]

# Setup and network construction

Open `W11_Dutch_Classroom.Rproj` after extracting the complete folder. Install
missing packages **before** class. This document runs two rank-zero chains; it
loads two rank-two chains estimated beforehand. The separate script
`scripts/estimate_rank2_before_class.R` contains the rank-two reproduction calls.
There are no automatic downloads, package installations, or substitutions for
missing fit files.

```{r setup}
# [I check packages without installing or upgrading anything during the lesson.]
required <- c("amen", "igraph", "posterior", "knitr")
missing <- required[!vapply(required, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(missing)) stop(paste("I need these packages before class:", paste(missing, collapse = ", ")))
library(amen)

# [These relative paths work from the extracted project, not an isolated Rmd.]
manifest <- read.csv("DATA_MANIFEST.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
stopifnot(all(file.exists(manifest$file)))
if (!identical(unname(tools::md5sum(manifest$file)), manifest$md5)) {
  stop("A supplied input differs from its recorded copy. I restore the original input rather than alter its fingerprint.")
}
reference <- readRDS("data/input_reference.rds")
nom <- read.csv("data/group36_like_nominations.csv", colClasses = "character", check.names = FALSE)
actors <- read.csv("data/group36_attributes.csv", colClasses = "character", check.names = FALSE)
ids <- nom$PPN
actors <- actors[match(ids, actors$node_id), , drop = FALSE]
stopifnot(identical(ids, actors$node_id), !anyDuplicated(ids), length(ids) == 16L)
sex <- as.integer(actors$sex)
age <- as.numeric(actors$age)
stopifnot(all(sex %in% 0:1), all(is.finite(age)))
nom[1:3, c("PPN", "group", "Q", "nomination1", "nomination2")]
```

[The recorded render warned that `amen` was built under R 4.6.1 while this
session used R 4.6.0. That warning did not stop this run. It is not a guarantee
of compatibility on every computer; I retain warnings and complete the preflight rather than suppress them or require everyone to upgrade.]

The archive calls the field `sex`; the article's Table 3 note (p. 7) and S4 Table
provide the published key `0 = female`, `1 = male`. I use that documentary key
for the plots, not behavioral differences as evidence of coding.
[Matching recorded codes is unchanged by reversing their labels. These two
categories are not an exhaustive measure of gender.]

The codebook maps `9999` to `NA`. In group 36, those entries occur after each
student's nonempty list, so I treat them as unused slots. I do not infer that a
fully empty response elsewhere means observed zero nominations. One original
list repeats `1042 -> 1046`; I keep the raw entries and count that ordered
relationship once.

```{r construct-network}
# [Rows send and columns receive; unique() gives a binary nomination per pair.]
Y <- matrix(0L, length(ids), length(ids), dimnames = list(ids, ids))
listed_slots <- 0L
for (i in seq_along(ids)) {
  targets <- unname(unlist(nom[i, paste0("nomination", 1:30)], use.names = FALSE))
  targets <- targets[targets != "9999"]
  stopifnot(length(targets) > 0L, all(targets %in% ids), !any(targets == ids[i]))
  listed_slots <- listed_slots + length(targets)
  Y[i, match(unique(targets), ids)] <- 1L
}
diag(Y) <- NA_integer_  # [Self-pairs do not enter the likelihood.]
stopifnot(identical(Y, reference$Y), listed_slots == 97L)

# [A has a zero diagonal for graph calculations; Y keeps its excluded diagonal.]
A <- Y
diag(A) <- 0L
g <- igraph::graph_from_adjacency_matrix(A, mode = "directed", weighted = NULL, diag = FALSE)
stopifnot(identical(igraph::V(g)$name, ids))
```

[The released roster is complete for the selected inputs, not independently
verified against an enrollment census. I selected this group for response and
attribute completeness before fitting, not for coefficients or model fit.]

# Describe and visualize the network

## Size, reciprocity, and transitivity

[An actor is a student. A dyad is a pair of students; this directed matrix has
240 ordered non-self entries within 120 unordered student pairs. `Y[i, j]`
records whether student i nominates student j. Out-degree counts nominations
sent; in-degree counts nominations received. Directed density divides ties by
n(n - 1), while mutual undirected density divides edges by n(n - 1)/2.
Reciprocity is the fraction of directed nominations with a reverse nomination.
Directed transitivity here is the fraction of distinct-student two-paths
`i -> j -> k` with `i -> k`. I state the denominator rather than treating
all transitivity definitions as equivalent (`igraph` documentation).]

```{r descriptive-statistics}
n_students <- igraph::vcount(g)
n_ties <- igraph::ecount(g)
out_degree <- igraph::degree(g, mode = "out", loops = FALSE)
in_degree <- igraph::degree(g, mode = "in", loops = FALSE)
reciprocated_fraction <- igraph::reciprocity(g, ignore.loops = TRUE, mode = "default")

# [A %*% A counts directed two-paths. Removing its diagonal keeps i different from k.]
two_paths <- A %*% A
diag(two_paths) <- 0
n_two_paths <- sum(two_paths)
n_closed_paths <- sum(two_paths * A)
directed_transitivity <- n_closed_paths / n_two_paths

# [This separate undirected graph follows the paper's mutual-tie rule.]
M <- A * t(A)
g_mutual <- igraph::graph_from_adjacency_matrix(M, mode = "undirected", weighted = NULL, diag = FALSE)
mutual_pairs <- igraph::ecount(g_mutual)
mutual_density <- igraph::edge_density(g_mutual, loops = FALSE)
mutual_transitivity <- igraph::transitivity(g_mutual, type = "global")
descriptives <- data.frame(
  measure = c("Students", "Directed ties", "Directed density", "Reciprocated fraction of ties",
              "Directed transitivity: closed two-path fraction", "Mutual undirected edges",
              "Mutual-network density", "Mutual-network global transitivity"),
  value = c(n_students, n_ties, igraph::edge_density(g, loops = FALSE), reciprocated_fraction,
            directed_transitivity, mutual_pairs, mutual_density, mutual_transitivity))
knitr::kable(descriptives, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

[There are `r n_ties` directed nominations and `r mutual_pairs` mutual pairs.
Thus `r 2 * mutual_pairs` of the `r n_ties` nominations are reciprocated:
`r round(100 * reciprocated_fraction, 1)`%. Of `r n_two_paths` directed two-paths,
`r n_closed_paths` are transitively closed. Neither number is the model's residual
`rho`. The mutual graph's density is lower because it excludes one-way liking.]

For `g_mutual`, global transitivity is **three times the number of triangles
divided by the number of connected triples**, where a triple has two mutual
edges sharing a student (`igraph::transitivity`). It is not AME's centered,
standardized `trans.dep`, which appears later.

## Degree distributions

```{r outdegree-distribution, fig.alt="Distribution of outgoing liking nominations among all sixteen students."}
barplot(table(factor(out_degree, levels = 0:(n_students - 1))),
  xlab = "Outgoing nominations", ylab = "Number of students", main = "Sending activity")
```

[Outgoing degree counts how many classmates each student nominates; it is not a
measure of helpfulness.]

```{r indegree-distribution, fig.alt="Distribution of incoming liking nominations among all sixteen students."}
barplot(table(factor(in_degree, levels = 0:(n_students - 1))),
  xlab = "Incoming nominations", ylab = "Number of students", main = "Receiving nominations")
```

[Incoming degree counts how often a student is nominated. One student receives
no nominations but sends nine, so that student is not an isolate. This is liking
popularity, not the study's separately measured perceived-popularity item.]

## Sociogram

```{r sociogram, fig.height=7, fig.alt="All sixteen students and 96 directed liking nominations. Circles and squares repeat the recorded sex coding shown by the colors; the key sits below the network."}
# [I keep the layout seed and algorithm. Only the display and its key change.]
sex_colors <- c("#56B4E9", "#E69F00")
sex_shapes <- c("circle", "square")
node_colors <- sex_colors[sex + 1L]
key_text <- c("Code 0: female (published key)", "Code 1: male (published key)")
set.seed(50836)
layout_xy <- igraph::layout_with_fr(g)
old_par <- par(mar = c(.5, .5, 2.5, .5))
# [Rescaled nodes occupy -1 to 1; the lower strip is reserved for the key.]
plot(g, layout = layout_xy, rescale = TRUE, ylim = c(-1.65, 1.1),
     vertex.color = node_colors, vertex.shape = sex_shapes[sex + 1L],
     vertex.size = 16, vertex.label = ids, vertex.label.family = "sans",
     vertex.label.cex = .8, vertex.label.color = "black",
     edge.arrow.size = .4, edge.curved = .12, edge.color = "grey50",
     main = "Who nominates whom in archive group 36?")
legend(x = 0, y = -1.32, xjust = .5, yjust = .5, legend = key_text,
       pch = c(21, 22), pt.bg = sex_colors, pt.cex = 1.4, bty = "n", cex = .8)
par(old_par)
```

[Arrows preserve all 96 nominations. Layout positions are a visual arrangement,
not a measured social distance or fitted latent space. Color and shape show
recorded categories; apparent grouping does not establish a causal preference.]

# Model the nominations in steps

## Step 1: Define the predictors and model

```{r predictors}
Xdyad <- array(0, dim = c(length(ids), length(ids), 2L),
  dimnames = list(ids, ids, c("same_recorded_sex", "age_absdiff_years")))
Xdyad[, , "same_recorded_sex"] <- 1 * outer(sex, sex, "==")
Xdyad[, , "age_absdiff_years"] <- abs(outer(age, age, "-"))
stopifnot(identical(Xdyad, reference$Xdyad))
dim(Xdyad)
```

[The first layer compares recorded categories; the second measures age difference
in years. Row and column order is identical to `Y`. `Xrow = NULL` and `Xcol = NULL`
omit measured sender/receiver predictors, not their latent random effects.]

For a binary probit model, `Y[i,j] = 1` when the latent propensity is positive:

**z<sub>ij</sub> = β<sub>0</sub> + β<sub>s</sub>same<sub>ij</sub> + β<sub>a</sub>|age<sub>i</sub> − age<sub>j</sub>| + a<sub>i</sub> + b<sub>j</sub> + u<sub>i</sub><sup>T</sup>v<sub>j</sub> + ε<sub>ij</sub>.**

| Component | Meaning in this classroom | Code/result |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Measured coefficients | Conditional association with matching sex code and age difference | `Xdyad`, `BETA` |
| Sender effect | Residual tendency to nominate classmates | `rvar`, `APM`, variance `va` |
| Receiver effect | Residual tendency to receive nominations | `cvar`, `BPM`, variance `vb` |
| Sender–receiver covariance | Association between the same student's two tendencies | `cab` |
| Residual reciprocity | Correlation between opposite-direction latent errors within a pair | `dcor`, `rho` |
| Multiplicative contribution | Higher-order patterns beyond the predictors and additive/dyadic terms | `R`, `U`, `V`, `UVPM` |

INA §10.5 calls AME a latent-factor model. Week 10 introduced Euclidean distance
(slide 4) and a bilinear inner-product representation (slides 20–21). These calls
use separate sender/receiver vectors, not a Euclidean-distance term. Additive
and dyadic components represent actor heterogeneity and reciprocity; multiplicative
effects can represent higher-order patterns (Dorff et al., 2020, pp. 484–485;
Minhas et al., 2019; Hoff, 2021).

[The readings may place a diagonal scaling matrix between factors; the installed
directed implementation computes `U %*% t(V)`. That scaling can be absorbed
algebraically into unrestricted vectors without establishing identical priors.
`R = 0` removes only the multiplicative part. `R = 2` can represent shared-partner
and triadic patterns but does not guarantee transitivity or identify a trait.
`R` is the multiplicative dimension, not a distance dimension or mixture-group
count. The residual variance is fixed at one for probit identification. Given
model parameters and latent effects, different unordered residual pairs are
independent, but opposite directions within a pair may correlate through `rho`.
`prior = list()` retains the package's default, data-calibrated priors.]

## Step 2: Fit two rank-zero chains live

[These calls run both when I execute the chunk and when I knit the lesson.
In the October 29 run they took 108.63 and 105.84 seconds, about 3.57 minutes
combined; the table prints the times for the current run. Other computers may
differ. A chain is a sequence of simulated parameter values. I discard the
first 10,000 iterations (`burn`), run 50,000 more (`nscan`), and retain every
25th (`odens`): 2,000 saved draws per chain. Saving less often does not make
those draws independent. I keep the checked settings (`amen::ame`, version 1.4.5).]

```{r fit-rank-zero}
RNGkind("Mersenne-Twister", "Inversion", "Rejection")
seeds0 <- c(50836101L, 50836102L)
r0_execution <- "estimated_in_this_session"
R0 <- vector("list", 2L)
runtime0 <- numeric(2L)
for (j in seq_along(seeds0)) {
  cat("I fit rank-zero chain", j, "with seed", seeds0[j], "\n")
  runtime0[j] <- system.time({
    R0[[j]] <- amen::ame(
      Y = Y, Xdyad = Xdyad, Xrow = NULL, Xcol = NULL,
      family = "bin", R = 0, rvar = TRUE, cvar = TRUE, dcor = TRUE,
      intercept = TRUE, symmetric = FALSE, prior = list(),
      seed = seeds0[j], burn = 10000, nscan = 50000, odens = 25,
      plot = FALSE, print = FALSE, gof = TRUE
    )
  })[["elapsed"]]
}
data.frame(chain = 1:2, seed = seeds0, seconds = runtime0,
           retained = vapply(R0, function(f) nrow(f$BETA), integer(1)))
```

[These two chains estimate the same model with different random-number seeds.
They are not two different classrooms. The package uses data-based starts;
different seeds are not deliberately dispersed starting values. A chain count
alone does not establish adequate sampling.]

## Step 3: Load two rank-two chains estimated beforehand

```{r load-rank-two-estimated-beforehand}
# [These fits already exist. This chunk does not run rank-two estimation.]
preestimated <- readRDS("data/rank2_preestimated.rds")
stopifnot(identical(preestimated$inputs$Y, Y),
          identical(preestimated$inputs$Xdyad, Xdyad), length(preestimated$fits) == 2L)
R2 <- preestimated$fits
stopifnot(all(vapply(R2, function(f) nrow(f$BETA), integer(1)) == 8000L))
data.frame(chain = 1:2, seed = preestimated$seeds,
           retained = vapply(R2, function(f) nrow(f$BETA), integer(1)))
```

I use the first two numbered chains from the longer rank-two run, not a pair
chosen for attractive results. Each used 10,000 burn-in iterations and 200,000
later iterations, saving every 25th. The four-chain background checks remain
in my authoring records; every table below uses **two chains per model**. The
rank-zero and rank-two budgets differ, but their data and model components other
than multiplicative rank are the same.

## Step 4: Check sampling and summarize the estimates

```{r summarize-two-chains}
# [Each column of x is a chain; I do not concatenate chains before calculating R-hat.]
summarize_model <- function(fits, model) {
  parameters <- c(colnames(fits[[1]]$BETA), "va", "vb", "cab", "rho")
  rows <- lapply(parameters, function(p) {
    x <- sapply(fits, function(f) {
      if (p %in% colnames(f$BETA)) f$BETA[, p] else f$VC[, p]
    })
    data.frame(model = model, parameter = p, mean = mean(x),
      lower = unname(quantile(x, .025)), upper = unname(quantile(x, .975)),
      rhat = posterior::rhat(x), bulk_ess = posterior::ess_bulk(x),
      tail_ess = posterior::ess_tail(x), mcse_over_sd = posterior::mcse_mean(x) / sd(c(x)))
  })
  do.call(rbind, rows)
}
summary_table <- rbind(summarize_model(R0, "R = 0"), summarize_model(R2, "R = 2"))
stopifnot(all(vapply(c(R0, R2), function(f) all(f$VC[, "ve"] == 1), logical(1))))
knitr::kable(summary_table[, c("model", "parameter", "rhat", "bulk_ess", "tail_ess", "mcse_over_sd")],
             digits = c(0, 0, 4, 0, 0, 3), row.names = FALSE)
flag <- with(summary_table, !is.finite(rhat) | rhat >= 1.01 | bulk_ess < 400 |
                              tail_ess < 400 | mcse_over_sd > .05)
if (any(flag)) warning("I inspect the flagged summaries; I do not change the pair or discard a chain.")
```

[**Sampling check:** R-hat near one and sufficiently large effective sample
sizes are reassuring, but do not prove convergence. These diagnostics concern
the saved parameter draws, not the number of students. `mcse_over_sd` measures
simulation error in a posterior mean relative to its posterior standard
deviation; I exclude `ve` only after verifying that it is fixed at one.]


```{r coefficients}
coefficient_rows <- summary_table$parameter %in% colnames(R0[[1]]$BETA)
knitr::kable(summary_table[coefficient_rows, c("model", "parameter", "mean", "lower", "upper")],
             digits = 3, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Probit coefficients and central 95% credible intervals")
# [This small lookup keeps the narrative tied to the actual results above.]
value <- function(model, parameter, column = "mean") {
  summary_table[summary_table$model == model & summary_table$parameter == parameter, column]
}
interval_text <- function(model, parameter) {
  paste0("[", sprintf("%.3f", value(model, parameter, "lower")), ", ",
         sprintf("%.3f", value(model, parameter, "upper")), "]")
}
```

[**Matching recorded sex:** The coefficients are
`r sprintf("%.3f", value("R = 0", "same_recorded_sex.dyad"))` for R0 and
`r sprintf("%.3f", value("R = 2", "same_recorded_sex.dyad"))` for R2.
Both indicate a positive conditional association between matching recorded
sex codes and liking nominations, not a percentage-point effect or proof
of a causal preference.]

[**Age difference:** The estimated coefficients are
`r sprintf("%.3f", value("R = 0", "age_absdiff_years.dyad"))` for R0 and
`r sprintf("%.3f", value("R = 2", "age_absdiff_years.dyad"))` for R2.
Both credible intervals include zero, so the association remains uncertain
in this classroom. These are probit coefficients, not odds ratios.]

```{r activity-popularity-reciprocity}
variance_rows <- summary_table$parameter %in% c("va", "vb", "cab", "rho")
knitr::kable(summary_table[variance_rows, c("model", "parameter", "mean", "lower", "upper")],
             digits = 3, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Sender/receiver components and residual reciprocity")
```

[**Activity and popularity:** `va` and `vb` measure remaining differences
in students' latent tendencies to send and receive nominations. For R2,
their posterior means are `r sprintf("%.3f", value("R = 2", "va"))` and
`r sprintf("%.3f", value("R = 2", "vb"))`. These are not observed degree
variances.]

[**Covariance:** `cab` describes the association between the same student's
latent sending and receiving tendencies. The R2 interval is
`r interval_text("R = 2", "cab")`, indicating a negative conditional
association in this model, not a personal trait or causal mechanism.]

[**Residual reciprocity:** `rho` measures the remaining association
between opposite-direction latent errors, not the observed reciprocated-tie
fraction. Its R2 interval is `r interval_text("R = 2", "rho")`, which
includes zero. The installed sampler also has a boundary at 0.995;
the model's residual reciprocity remains uncertain.]

## Step 5: Visualize the multiplicative effects

[Each row of `U` is a sending profile and each row of `V` a receiving profile.
I show the **first numbered R2 chain**. The returned matrices form an SVD-based
rank-two approximation to its mean product `UVPM`, not complete factor-draw
histories. I do not average unaligned coordinates across chains or identify
an arbitrary axis with a measured student trait.]

```{r sending-factors, fig.alt="Sending profiles from the first numbered R2 chain. Colors and shapes identify recorded sex codes; Factor 2 uses an expanded display scale, and the same coordinate limits are used for V."}
U <- R2[[1]]$U
V <- R2[[1]]$V
stopifnot(ncol(U) == 2L, ncol(V) == 2L,
          identical(rownames(U), ids), identical(rownames(V), ids))
xlim <- grDevices::extendrange(c(U[, 1], V[, 1]), f = .12)
ylim <- grDevices::extendrange(c(U[, 2], V[, 2]), f = .18)
sex_pch <- c(21, 22)[sex + 1L]
# [Only text placement changes; I do not move the fitted coordinates.]
u_label_pos <- setNames(rep(3, length(ids)), ids)
u_label_pos["1038"] <- 4
plot(U[, 1], U[, 2], pch = sex_pch, bg = node_colors, cex = 1.4,
     xlim = xlim, ylim = ylim, xlab = "Factor 1",
     ylab = "Factor 2 (expanded display scale)", main = "U: sending profiles (R2 chain 1)")
abline(h = 0, v = 0, lty = 3)
text(U[, 1], U[, 2], labels = ids, pos = u_label_pos, cex = .75)
legend("bottomleft", legend = key_text, pch = c(21, 22), pt.bg = sex_colors,
       bty = "n", cex = .75)
```

[The contribution in this rank-two display is the **sum**
u<sub>i1</sub>v<sub>j1</sub> + u<sub>i2</sub>v<sub>j2</sub>.
Same signs make the first product positive; opposite signs make it negative.
The second product can reverse the total, especially near zero on Factor 1.
The sender–receiver contribution is not their Euclidean distance.]

```{r receiving-factors, fig.alt="Receiving profiles from the same R2 chain, with the same scales and color-and-shape key as U. Only crowded text labels are repositioned."}
v_label_pos <- setNames(rep(3, length(ids)), ids)
v_label_pos[c("1036", "1041")] <- 1
v_label_pos["1042"] <- 4
plot(V[, 1], V[, 2], pch = sex_pch, bg = node_colors, cex = 1.4,
     xlim = xlim, ylim = ylim, xlab = "Factor 1",
     ylab = "Factor 2 (expanded display scale)", main = "V: receiving profiles (R2 chain 1)")
abline(h = 0, v = 0, lty = 3)
text(V[, 1], V[, 2], labels = ids, pos = v_label_pos, cex = .75)
legend("bottomleft", legend = key_text, pch = c(21, 22), pt.bg = sex_colors,
       bty = "n", cex = .75)
```

[**Factor interpretation:** In this chain's mean-product summary, the
first singular value is approximately 28.93 and the second approximately
0.69, so the first component dominates this displayed summary.
This does not mean the fitted model is rank one or that the axes identify
measured personality traits. The factor plots represent model-based
sending and receiving patterns, not the sociogram's layout positions.]

## Step 6: Check all five network features

The default `amen` plot shows parameter traces and five predictive histograms.
I retain the unchanged package method and show the first numbered chain of each
model; the numerical table uses both chains. These single-chain panels do not
replace the two-chain diagnostics.

[Trace colors distinguish **parameters within one chain**, not different chains.
The VC panel follows `va`, `cab`, `vb`, `rho`, `ve`; the BETA panel follows the
intercept, matching-code coefficient, and age-difference coefficient. Colored
horizontal lines mark that chain's parameter medians. The gray zero line is in
the BETA panel. In each histogram the red vertical line is the observed statistic;
the bars describe saved replicated-network statistics and use a density scale
with omitted vertical-axis ticks (`amen::plot.ame`, version 1.4.5).]

```{r default-ame-r0, fig.width=8, fig.height=7.5, out.width="100%", dev.args=list(pointsize=14), fig.alt="Default amen plot for R0 chain 1, with parameter traces and all five predictive statistics. Each histogram marks the observed network with a red vertical line."}
plot(R0[[1]])
```

[For each histogram, locate the observed line and compare it with the whole
replicated distribution, not only with its center.]

```{r default-ame-r2, fig.width=8, fig.height=7.5, out.width="100%", dev.args=list(pointsize=14), fig.alt="Default amen plot for R2 chain 1, using the same five predictive statistics and observed references as the R0 plot."}
plot(R2[[1]])
```

| GOF label | Network feature |
|:--|:--|
| `sd.rowmean` | Standard deviation of outgoing nomination rates across students |
| `sd.colmean` | Standard deviation of incoming nomination rates across students |
| `dyad.dep` | Observed opposite-direction association; not residual `rho` |
| `cycle.dep` | Centered, standardized directed-cycle dependence |
| `trans.dep` | Centered, standardized transitive dependence; not the descriptive closure ratio |

[The central 95% **predictive interval** contains the middle 95% of a statistic
across the saved replicated networks. It concerns replicated data, whereas a
credible interval concerns a parameter. The installed implementation returns
five GOF statistics even though the brief help description mentions four.]

```{r all-five-gof-table}
predictive_table <- function(fits, label) {
  observed <- fits[[1]]$GOF[1, ]
  stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(observed, fits[[2]]$GOF[1, ])))
  # [Row 1 is observed; I exclude it from all replicated-draw calculations.]
  draws <- do.call(rbind, lapply(fits, function(f) f$GOF[-1, , drop = FALSE]))
  intervals <- apply(draws, 2, quantile, probs = c(.025, .975))
  share <- colMeans(sweep(draws, 2, observed, ">="))
  data.frame(model = label, statistic = names(observed), observed = unname(observed),
    replicated_mean = colMeans(draws), lower = intervals[1, ], upper = intervals[2, ],
    rep_ge_obs = unname(share), row.names = NULL)
}
gof_table <- rbind(predictive_table(R0, "R = 0"), predictive_table(R2, "R = 2"))
knitr::kable(gof_table, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Both chains: observed values, replicated means, central 95% intervals, and replicated shares at least as large as observed")
gof_value <- function(model, statistic, column) {
  gof_table[gof_table$model == model & gof_table$statistic == statistic, column]
}
```

[**Predictive fit:** All five observed statistics fall within both models'
central 95% predictive intervals, but coverage alone does not establish
good fit. For `trans.dep`, approximately
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * gof_value("R = 0", "trans.dep", "rep_ge_obs"))`%
of R0 replications and
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * gof_value("R = 2", "trans.dep", "rep_ge_obs"))`%
of R2 replications reach the observed value, suggesting that R2 better
reproduces this particular feature. R2 is not closer for every feature;
these are in-sample descriptive comparisons, not causal findings or
formal model-selection results.]

# Connect the results to classroom cohesion

Van den Bos et al. (2018, p. 3) measure cohesion using mutual liking,
whereas my directed network also retains one-way nominations.

[**What these results suggest about cohesion:** In group 36,
`r 2 * mutual_pairs` of `r n_ties` directed nominations are reciprocated
(`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * reciprocated_fraction)`%), and
`r n_closed_paths` of `r n_two_paths` directed two-paths are closed
(`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * directed_transitivity)`%), suggesting
substantial mutuality and local closure among the recorded classroom ties.
Requiring mutual nominations reduces density from
`r sprintf("%.3f", igraph::edge_density(g, loops = FALSE))` to
`r sprintf("%.3f", mutual_density)`, showing that many nominations are
one-way, including the nine sent by student 1040.
These patterns are consistent with some local cohesion, but they do not
establish how this classroom compares with other classrooms or whether
cohesion causes helping, trust, or supportive relationships.]
